=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Why haven’t farm animals evolved against humans? A biologist explains why there won’t be a chicken uprising anytime soon ===

[Source 1 — theconversation.com] (URL: https://theconversation.com/why-havent-farm-animals-evolved-against-humans-a-biologist-explains-why-there-wont-be-a-chicken-uprising-anytime-soon-291839):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Why haven’t farm animals evolved against humans? A biologist explains why there won’t be a chicken uprising anytime soon

From domesticated foxes to tuskless elephants, humans have directly and indirectly influenced the evolution of a wide range of animals.

Actual Article Body:
Share article

Print article

Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.

Why haven’t farm animals evolved to protect themselves against humans? – Sarang, age 15, Latur, Maharashtra, India

Have you ever wondered why dogs get the zoomies or wag their tails? One answer comes from a rather unexpected source: foxes.

A team of scientists bred captured silver foxes for tameness, choosing the least fearful and aggressive animals to become parents. They repeated this process with each litter of pups, avoiding any training and limiting their exposure to people.

Within six generations, the foxes began to show some familiar, doglike behaviors. Some wagged their tails as people approached, licked their hands and even liked to be petted.

These silver foxes are a remarkable example of selective breeding, where people choose animals with particular traits to produce the next generation of animals.

Selective breeding is the driving force behind domestication: the process through which animal populations adapted to life alongside people over many generations. Dogs are considered the first animals that humans domesticated, originally descending from wolves.

Another team of scientists studied the genes of ancient animals to understand how domestication has shaped farm animals over time. They examined the genetics of a wide range of traits, from coat color in goats and horses to aggression and egg production in chickens.

Farmers might selectively breed chickens for more eggs, or cows for more milk. They may also favor calmer animals because they are easier to handle. Because animals with these traits are chosen more frequently by farmers for breeding, their genes have a better chance of reaching the next generation.

This process is domestication in action: Inherited traits such as tameness, producing more food or having a coat color preferred by people become common over generations.

Farm animals that are aggressive or don’t produce much food may be less useful to humans, thereby “protecting” themselves from being used by people. But with people in charge, these animals will also likely be excluded from breeding and have less of a chance of passing their genes on.

On the farm, people hold all the power. Because of the process of domestication through selective breeding, farm animals cannot evolve to protect themselves from humans.

People can influence evolution in the wild even without deciding which animals to breed.

Animals with traits that help them evade humans who are trying to hunt or capture them will tend to pass on their genes to the next generation. This means that, in the wild, animal populations may evolve more protective characteristics, since people aren’t directly involved in selecting which animals will breed and pass on their genes.

Consider the elephants of Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique, a species I study in my work as an evolutionary biologist. During the country’s civil war, poachers hunted large numbers of elephants for their ivory tusks.

Some females were naturally tuskless, making them less likely to be targeted. As a result, these tuskless females had a better chance of surviving, reproducing and passing on the genes associated with tusklessness. Over generations, tusklessness became more common in the population.

While these elephants did not deliberately evolve a defense against hunters, tusklessness provided a survival benefit. Therefore, evolution favored an existing trait that offered some protection.

From friendly foxes to tuskless elephants, human choices can shape how animal populations evolve. Sometimes people do this deliberately, by breeding animals for desired traits. Other times, human impact on the environment alone can change which animals survive and reproduce, and therefore shape how species evolve.

Next time your dog snuggles up, remember those foxes!

Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

Assistant Professor of Evolutionary Genomics, University of Tennessee

For 35 years, regional high school students in Western Australia have exhibited their art in this gallery. Here are five works you should see.

By Mietta Adams

ABC Arts

Topic:Visual Art

Emmasyn Dillon (right) won the Iluka Vision's top award for their mixed media sculpture. (Supplied: Abby Murray)

High school artists have been in the spotlight after 17-year-old student Jazz Lancaster Merton was crowned the 2026 Portrait Artist of the Year.

This month, secondary students in Western Australia's south-west region have had their chance to show their work in a professional setting, through a beloved community exhibition that has been running for 35 years.

Artist and arts educator Charlotte White, who was a judge at this year's Iluka Visions at Bunbury Regional Gallery, said it was an important launch pad for arts student careers.

Here are five artworks she says you should see at the exhibition:

Emmasyn Dillon's work won the Year 11 and 12 Best Overall Artwork at Iluka Visions. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

Emmasyn Dillon's mixed media sculpture received the Viewer's Choice Award and overall Best Year 11 and 12 Award.

White said she was captivated by the construction of the life-sized figure and the emotional depth to the two-sided sculpture.

"[It's amazing] to think about the technical skills to creating something like this, so not only thinking about a body sitting on a chair, but how that is going to be balanced with another figure coming out the back," she said.

"The more you look at this work, the more you can get out of it."

The dolls and their costumes were constructed by Remy Mathieson. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

One of White's favourite works was Remy Mathieson's small doll-sized rat dolls, made with resin, paint, textiles, leather and wood.

"She's gone as far as to create custom costumes and they have little trinkets in their jackets, and there's character backgrounds next to each doll talking about who they are and what they do," she said.

"I almost want to see a story or a movie or something that like moves on from just these characters — I want to know more about them."

Pia Mangano's work won the Year 11 and 12 3D Award. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

White said this work was selected for the best Year 11 and 12 3D Award because of its role as a thought-provoking and interactive conversational piece.

The question 'Does the inclusion of AI in art mean the end of human creativity?' is written under the sculpture and encourages viewers to ink their fingerprint under the 'yes' or 'no' column.

"It made me realise that these young artists are actually talking about big topics," White said.

"And it was really remarkable that they're not just creating art; they're inviting the audience to have a bit of a debate about things."

Beccy Mason's artwork titled All That Floats Away. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

The winner of the Year 9 and 10 Best Overall Artwork, All That Floats Away, was made out of cardboard, tissue paper, shellac, wire mesh and bamboo skewers.

White said it conveyed a sense of nostalgia and wonder.

"It had really a really interesting concept with a great use of those everyday materials and using them in a really interesting way," White said.

She also said the work was reminiscent of the renowned Japanese animation storytellers, Studio Ghibli.

"It had an imaginative, creative playfulness ... it's suspended and hanging within the gallery like it's sort of flying through."

Students from the centre collaborated on this bright and colourful work. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

White also highlighted this playful work of sticks wrapped in yarn, which was a collaboration between students at the Newton Moore Education Support Centre.

It's a Wrap won the Equity Award.

"I can imagine it was tricky for some to create this, but it's a really beautiful piece," White said.

"It's so colourful and textured; it's coming out from the wall and there's pom-poms and there's beads.

"We just really loved this work and how the students have created it together to create this really beautiful well-rounded piece."

Iluka Visions is at Bunbury Regional Gallery until November 15.
